# Borrowing and lifetimes {#sec-borrowing}

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
source("_common.R")
```

If every function took ownership of its arguments, a vector would be gone after the first call that used it. Most Rust functions borrow instead. They take a *reference*, written with `&`, use the value through it, and leave the owner with the value when they return. R does something similar behind your back: as `tracemem()` showed in @sec-ownership, a function that only reads its argument works on the caller's value without copying it. This chapter covers shared references, mutable references, the rules that keep them safe, and lifetimes, which are how the compiler checks that no reference outlives its value. The matching sections of the Rust book are "References and Borrowing" and "Validating References with Lifetimes" [@rustbook, secs. 4.2, 10.3].

## Shared references

Each version of `mean_of()` here reads a vector without changing it. The R function gets the caller's vector without a copy, and the Rust function takes a reference to it:

```{r}
#| label: r-borrow
mean_of <- function(values) sum(values) / length(values)

x <- c(2, 4, 4, 5)
tracemem(x)
mean_of(x)
mean_of(x[2:4])
x
```

```{rust}
#| label: rust-borrow
fn mean_of(values: &[f64]) -> f64 {
    let mut sum = 0.0;
    for value in values {
        sum = sum + value;
    }
    sum / values.len() as f64
}

fn main() {
    let x = vec![2.0, 4.0, 4.0, 5.0];
    println!("{}", mean_of(&x));
    println!("{}", mean_of(&x[1..]));
    println!("{:?}", x);
}
```

Writing `&x` creates a shared reference to `x`, and `mean_of(&x)` lends the vector to the function for the length of the call. Ownership stays with `x`, so the last line can still use it. The argument type, `&[f64]`, is the slice type from @sec-vectors: a reference to a run of `f64` values, which can be a whole vector or part of one. Passing `&x`, a `&Vec<f64>`, where a `&[f64]` is expected works because Rust converts the reference automatically. The conversion is called a *deref coercion*, and it also lets a `&String` go where a `&str` is expected (@sec-strings) [@rustbook, sec. 15.2]. It applies to a reference passed on its own, not to one inside another value, which is why @sec-cli calls `as_str()` on the `&String` inside an `Option`. The `for` loop goes over `values` without taking ownership of anything, because `values` is itself a reference. Each `value` in the loop is a `&f64`, a reference to one element. Rust defines `+` between an `f64` and a `&f64`, so `sum + value` works as written.

Any number of shared references to a value can exist at the same time, and none of them can change it. The exceptions are types designed to be changed through shared references, such as the `RefCell` in @sec-environments. A function that takes `&[f64]` can't modify the vector it was given, and the compiler checks that.

::: {.callout-tip title="The same idea in R"}
In the R version, `tracemem()` printed nothing for `mean_of(x)`: R passed the function the caller's vector, not a copy, because `mean_of()` never changed it. In effect, an R function that only reads its arguments is borrowing them. Rust makes that a promise in the function's signature, and the compiler holds the function to it.
:::

References have already appeared several times:

- `&self` in a method (@sec-structs) is a shared reference to the value the method was called on. A method that takes `self` without the `&`, like `add()` in @sec-operators, takes ownership instead.
- `&str` (@sec-strings) is a shared reference to text. A `String` owns its text; a `&str` borrows it.
- `&dyn Distribution` (@sec-generics) is a shared reference to a value of any type that implements the trait.
- `println!` borrows the values it prints, which is why the move errors in @sec-ownership spoke of a "borrow of moved value".

## Mutable references

A function that changes a value it doesn't own takes a mutable reference, `&mut`:

```{rust}
#| label: rust-mut-ref
fn scale(values: &mut [f64], factor: f64) {
    for i in 0..values.len() {
        values[i] = values[i] * factor;
    }
}

fn main() {
    let mut x = vec![1.0, 2.0, 3.0];
    scale(&mut x, 10.0);
    println!("{:?}", x);
}
```

The call `scale(&mut x, 10.0)` lends `x` to `scale()` with permission to change it, and the change is visible to the caller after the call. Both sides have to say so: the function's argument type is `&mut [f64]`, and the caller writes `&mut x`, which it can do only because `x` is declared `mut`. Leaving out any of the three `mut`s is a compile error.

An R function can't do this to a vector. As @sec-ownership showed, a change to an argument is made to a copy, so R code returns the changed vector and assigns it back. Environments are the exception, and @sec-environments covers them.

To change a plain number through a reference, put `*` in front of the reference to reach the value it points to:

```{rust}
#| label: rust-deref
fn add_one(count: &mut i32) {
    *count = *count + 1;
}

fn main() {
    let mut n = 0;
    add_one(&mut n);
    add_one(&mut n);
    println!("{n}");
}
```

In `add_one()`, `*count` is the `i32` that `count` refers to: `n` in `main()`. Indexing, field access, and method calls follow references on their own, which is why `scale()` could write `values[i]`. You need `*` mostly for numbers and other small values.

The `fmt()` method in @sec-display took `f: &mut fmt::Formatter`. That's a mutable reference too: `write!` adds text to the formatter, so `fmt()` needs permission to change it.

## The borrowing rules

At any moment, a value can have either any number of shared references or exactly one mutable reference, but not both [@rustbook, sec. 4.2]. Here a shared reference into a vector is still in use when the code tries to change the vector:

```{rust}
#| label: rust-borrow-conflict
#| error: true
let mut x = vec![1.0, 2.0, 3.0];
let first = &x[0];
x.push(4.0);
println!("{first}");
```

The call `x.push(4.0)` needs a mutable reference to `x`, but `first` still refers to one of its elements. The rule prevents a real bug. When a vector runs out of reserved room, `push()` gets a larger block of memory, which can mean moving the elements and freeing the old block. That would leave `first` pointing at freed memory. In C, that's a classic source of crashes and corrupted data. Rust rejects the program before it runs.

A borrow lasts until the reference's last use, not until the end of the block. Use `first` before the `push()`, and the program compiles:

```{rust}
#| label: rust-borrow-ends
let mut x = vec![1.0, 2.0, 3.0];
let first = &x[0];
println!("{first}");
x.push(4.0);
println!("{:?}", x);
```

The same rule rejects two mutable references to one value at once, `let a = &mut x;` followed by `let b = &mut x;` while `a` is still in use, because two parts of the code changing the same value can step on each other.

::: {.callout-note title="An R habit to drop in Rust"}
R never runs into this conflict, because R has no references into a vector. In R, `first <- x[1]` creates a new vector holding a copy of the value, and changing `x` afterward can't affect it. In Rust, `&x[0]` points into `x` without copying, and the compiler makes sure `x` doesn't change while anything points into it. When you need a value that's independent of the vector, copy it: `let first = x[0];` copies the `f64`, because `f64` is `Copy`.
:::

## Lifetimes

A reference must not outlive the value it refers to. Here `x` is dropped at the end of the inner block while `r` still refers to it:

```{rust}
#| label: rust-lifetime-error
#| error: true
let r;
{
    let x = vec![1.0, 2.0, 3.0];
    r = &x;
}
println!("{:?}", r);
```

The span of code during which a reference is valid is its *lifetime*. The compiler checks every reference's lifetime against the scope of the value it borrows, and the error shows both: `x` is dropped at the closing brace, and `r` is used after that.

::: {.callout-warning title="Where the analogy breaks"}
This error can't happen in R. R's garbage collector keeps a value alive as long as anything refers to it, so a reference can never outlive its value. Rust has no garbage collector. Each value is freed when its owner goes out of scope (@sec-ownership), so the compiler checks instead that every reference stops being used before then.
:::

Most of the time, lifetimes are worked out without any help. A function that takes one reference and returns one, such as `fn largest(values: &[f64]) -> &f64`, needs no annotation: the compiler assumes the result borrows from the argument. That assumption is one of a few *lifetime elision* rules that cover most functions [@rustbook, sec. 10.3]. With two reference arguments, the compiler can't guess which one the result borrows from:

```{rust}
#| label: rust-missing-lifetime
#| error: true
fn longer(a: &str, b: &str) -> &str {
    if a.len() >= b.len() { a } else { b }
}

fn main() {
    println!("{}", longer("normal", "uniform"));
}
```

The fix is the one the compiler suggests, a named lifetime:

```{rust}
#| label: rust-lifetime
fn longer<'a>(a: &'a str, b: &'a str) -> &'a str {
    if a.len() >= b.len() { a } else { b }
}

fn main() {
    println!("{}", longer("normal", "uniform"));
}
```

The `'a` in the signature is a lifetime parameter. It's declared in angle brackets like the type parameters of @sec-generics, and the leading apostrophe marks it as a lifetime. The signature says that the result is valid for as long as both arguments are, a span it names `'a`. The annotation doesn't change how long anything lives. It describes how the result relates to the arguments, so the compiler can check every call to `longer()` against it.

Every call has to respect that relationship. This one uses the result after `b` is dropped at the end of the inner block:

```{rust}
#| label: rust-lifetime-scope
#| error: true
fn longer<'a>(a: &'a str, b: &'a str) -> &'a str {
    if a.len() >= b.len() { a } else { b }
}

fn main() {
    let a = String::from("normal distribution");
    let result;
    {
        let b = String::from("uniform");
        result = longer(&a, &b);
    }
    println!("{result}");
}
```

This call would return `a`, the longer string, which is still alive. The compiler rejects it anyway, because it checks calls against the signature, not against what `longer()` happens to return, and the signature ties the result to both arguments. Moving the `println!` into the inner block, before `b` is dropped, fixes the program.

When a lifetime error is hard to resolve, returning an owned value is a legitimate way out. A function that returns a `String` or a `Vec<f64>` instead of a reference hands ownership to the caller, and there's no lifetime to check. It may cost a copy, usually a small price while you're learning.

::: {.callout-note title="Package developer notes: keeping R objects alive in C" collapse="true"}
C code faces R's version of the lifetime problem. An object that C code creates stays alive only while R knows it's in use. A pointer held in a C variable doesn't count, so the code must call `PROTECT()` on the object until it's done with it, and `UNPROTECT()` afterward. Otherwise the garbage collector can free the object while the code still points to it [@r-exts, sec. 5.9.1]. That's a lifetime managed by hand, and R only warns about a `PROTECT()`/`UNPROTECT()` imbalance after the fact. A Rust wrapper around an R object can protect it when the wrapper is created and release it when the wrapper is dropped (@sec-drop), so the release can't be forgotten. It can't use the protection stack for that, though: `UNPROTECT()` removes the most recent protections first, and Rust values aren't always dropped in that order. R also keeps a list of objects that the garbage collector must leave alone: `R_PreserveObject()` adds an object and `R_ReleaseObject()` removes it [@r-exts, sec. 5.9.1]. That list allows release in any order, so a wrapper can use it. Even then, an R error that jumps past the Rust code skips the drop, and the object is never released (@sec-drop).
:::

## Summary

| R | Rust |
|---------------------------|---------------------------|
| A function that only reads its argument doesn't copy it | `&T`: a shared reference, read-only for most types |
| A function can't change its caller's vector | `&mut T`: a mutable reference, marked at the call |
| `x[1]` copies the element | `&x[0]` points into `x`; `x[0]` copies an `f64` |
| No rule about who may change what | Many shared references or one mutable reference |
| The garbage collector keeps referenced values alive | A reference can't outlive its value |
| Nothing to annotate | Lifetime parameters such as `'a`, when the compiler can't infer them |
